   DBS chairman Peter Seah to hand reins over to Anthony Lim; bank’s Q3 net profit slips 5% to $2.8b
 Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox
 Chairman Peter Seah (left) will retire by the end of this year, and board member Anthony Lim will take over with effect from Jan 1, 2027.
 PHOTOS: LIANHE ZAOBAO FILE, DBS
 Angela Tan
 Published   Nov 05, 2026, 07:02 AM
 Updated   Nov 05, 2026, 10:29 AM
 Set as preferred source Listen Summarise 中文 DBS chairman Peter Seah will retire on Jan 1, 2027, and board member Anthony Lim will take over. Seah said DBS is now “in very capable hands.”
 DBS posted third-quarter 2026 net profit of $2.81 billion, down 5% from a year earlier. Nine-month net profit still rose 2% to a record $8.82 billion.
 Income and fees grew, but lower SORA cut margins. DBS declared 81 cents per share in third-quarter dividends, with CEO Tan Su Shan highlighting strong loans, deposits and wealth growth.
 AI generated
 SINGAPORE – DBS Group said its chairman Peter Seah will retire by the end of 2026 after 16 years at the helm of Singapore’s largest lender, with board member Anthony Lim taking over with effect from Jan 1, 2027.
 Seah, who has been the bank’s chairman since 2010, will be appointed as senior adviser for a year.
 DBS said Seah, 80, has provided steadfast leadership and strategic oversight as the bank pursued a strategy of digital transformation and growth in high-return businesses.
 It added he helped strengthen the bank’s connection to its heritage and played an important role in shaping the culture of the organisation, which today combines a longstanding sense of purpose with a strong customer focus and spirit of innovation.
 In an appreciation letter dated Nov 4, Temasek, a major DBS shareholder, paid tribute to Seah’s stewardship, describing his contribution to the bank as “profound and enduring”.
 The letter, jointly signed by Temasek chairman Teo Chee Hean and chief executive Dilhan Pillay Sandrasegara, highlighted the transformation of DBS under Seah’s chairmanship.
 When Seah took over in May 2010, he set out an ambition for DBS to become the Asian bank of choice for the “New Asia”, underpinned by a nine-point strategy anchored by the humility to serve and the confidence to lead.
 Sixteen years later, that ambition had been realised and more, Temasek said.
 DBS’ market capitalisation has grown more than sixfold since 2010, from about $35 billion to more than $200 billion, while its annual net profit rose from $2.65 billion to $11 billion in financial year 2025.
 Cumulative total shareholder returns, including dividends and bonus shares, exceeded 1,000 % over the period, equivalent to an annual compounded return of more than 16 % , Temasek said.
 It also credited Seah with giving management, led by former chief executive Piyush Gupta, the confidence and mandate to invest early in digital transformation, at a time when few banks were prepared to make the substantial financial, technological and people commitments required.
 The investments helped propel DBS into the ranks of the world’s leading digital banks. In 2016, it became the first bank to be named World’s Best Digital Bank by Euromoney.
 Gupta said: “Peter’s leadership was instrumental in DBS’ success over the past 16 years. He was the force behind our culture change, giving us the confidence to be bold and to invest for the future. As chairman, he balanced between guiding management while giving us elbow room to operate exceptionally well. I couldn’t have asked for a better partner and mentor.”
 Under Seah’s chairmanship, DBS also pursued a series of strategic acquisitions to strengthen its regional presence, including Societe Generale’s regional private banking business, ANZ’s Asia consumer and wealth franchise, Citi’s Taiwan consumer banking business and Lakshmi Vilas Bank in India.
 The bank also expanded its role in sustainable finance, with outstanding commitments of more than $100 billion, and established South-east Asia’s first science-based sectoral decarbonisation targets.
 Seah said that when he became DBS chairman, the world was only just emerging from the global financial crisis.
 Having completed the CEO transition to Tan Su Shan, the bank is now entering its next chapter from a position of strength.
 “I am therefore able to hand over the reins to Anthony with confidence, knowing that DBS is in very capable hands,” Seah said.
 Prior to his retirement from executive roles in 2017, Lim , 68, who has been serving on the bank’s board since April 2020, held senior leadership roles at GIC and Bankers Trust, with assignments in Singapore, London and New York.
 His global perspective, extensive financial markets experience and strong risk management expertise position him well to help DBS navigate an increasingly complex operating environment, the bank said.
 Temasek also expressed confidence in the incoming chairman, saying it was confident that DBS, under the leadership of Lim and Tan, would build on the foundations laid by Seah and Gupta.
 It singled out Seah’s role in overseeing the succession from Gupta to Tan, describing it as the culmination of more than a decade of deliberate talent development rather than a single event.
 Seah had also built a board that asked difficult questions and fostered a relationship with management grounded in trust and candour, Temasek added.
 His 15-year partnership with Gupta exemplified how a chairman and chief executive could bring out the best in each other and in the institution they led.
 Seah joined DBS’ board on Nov 16, 2009, and succeeded Koh Boon Hwee as chairman on May 1, 2010. Before joining DBS, he was president and chief executive of Singapore Technologies Group from 2001 until its merger into Temasek in December 2004.
 He had earlier spent much of his banking career at Citibank and Overseas Union Bank (OUB), where he became chief executive in 1991. He retired from OUB in September 2001 following its merger with United Overseas Bank.
 Quarterly earnings miss analysts’ forecast
 DBS reported a net profit of $2.81 billion for the third quarter of 2026. This is down 5% from $2.95 billion in the same period a year ago due to lower markets trading income amid unfavourable equity market conditions.
 The earnings missed the $2.95 billion consensus forecast in a Bloomberg survey of eight analysts.
 For the nine months, total income rose 2% to a new high of $17.9 billion, while net profit increased 2% to $8.82 billion.
 Group net interest income rose 4% year on year to $3.71 billion as proactive hedging and strong balance sheet growth more than offset the impact of a lower Singapore Overnight Rate Average (SORA) – the primary floating-rate benchmark for Singapore dollar loans, including floating-rate home and car loans.
 Group net interest margin declined nine basis points to 1.87%.
 Net fee income rose 6% to $1.43 billion. Wealth management fees increased 9% from a high base a year ago to $864 million, supported by growth in assets under management. Transaction services fees recorded a new high, while loan-related and card fees also increased.
 The board declared a total dividend of 81 cents a share for the third quarter, comprising an ordinary dividend of 66 cents a share and a capital return dividend of 15 cents a share.
 This takes the total dividend for the nine months to $2.43 a share, comprising ordinary dividends of $1.98 a share and capital return dividends of 45 cents a share.
 DBS CEO Tan said: “We turned in another quarter of strong franchise growth, with robust increases in loans, deposits and wealth assets. Nine-month net profit reached a record and return on equity was 17% despite average SORA having halved from a year ago and heightened geopolitical uncertainty.
 “The performance reflected our ability to capture structural opportunities across wealth management and institutional banking.”
 For the second quarter of 2026, DBS’ net profit rose 9% to a record $3.08 billion, as it leant on its wealth management business, treasury sales and trading income to drive growth.
